description: Take the Rijksmuseum apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the building: Pierre Cuypers's controversial cathedral of Dutch art, the tunnel through its middle, and the Night Watch at the end of the Gallery of Honour.

hotspots.text: The public passage runs straight through the building's central axis. Cyclists ride through the museum itself, one of Amsterdam's most photographed oddities.

hotspots.text: Stained glass was part of Cuypers's total decorative programme of tile pictures, mosaics and wall paintings. W.F. Dixon won the stained glass commission in the 1876 decoration contest.

hotspots.text: The building is two squares, each with an atrium court at its centre. The glass roofs over the courts date from the 2003-2013 renovation, which removed the floors built into them in the 1960s.

hotspots.text: The museum contains its own art library, the largest art history library in the Netherlands, rising through several storeys with a cast-iron spiral stair.

intro: Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum is Pierre Cuypers's 1885 cathedral of Dutch art: red brick, towers, and a bicycle tunnel straight through the middle. This is how a controversial building became the nation's museum.
page_title: Rijksmuseum Amsterdam: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: Pierre Cuypers came second in the 1863 design contest for a new national museum, when no entry was judged good enough. He won the new contest in 1876 and spent nine years building it. His design refused to choose a style: Gothic church architecture (towers, large circular windows) fused with Renaissance civic architecture (rectangular windows, roofs, dormers). The result in red brick with stone detailing was immediately controversial. Protestant critics found it too Gothic, too medieval, too Roman Catholic for a national museum. King William III reportedly refused to lay the first brick or perform the opening, declaring he would not set foot in that monastery. A separate contest chose the decoration: B. van Hove and Frantz Vermeylen for the sculptures, Georg Sturm for the tile panels and painting, W.F. Dixon for the stained glass. Cuypers built it anyway, and it opened on 13 July 1885.
sections.caption: The Rijksmuseum from the Museumplein.
sections.credit: Voytikof, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: A cathedral nobody asked for

sections.body: Cuypers organized the building as two squares, each with an atrium court at its centre. Through the central axis he cut a public tunnel with entrances at ground level, so the city could walk, and later cycle, straight through the museum. Above the tunnel on the second floor runs the Gallery of Honour, the ceremonial spine of the collection, entered through the Great Hall (Voorhal). The building also contained a library, the largest art history library in the Netherlands. A separate fragment building, added in 1890 southwest of the museum and later branded the Philips wing, displayed the history of Dutch architecture in salvaged pieces.
sections.caption: The Cuypers Library reading room.
sections.credit: Siepke van Keulen, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: Two squares and a tunnel

sections.body: The museum's 80 galleries tell 800 years of Dutch art in a single chronological sweep, from 1200 to 2000, and the sweep ends at the Night Watch. Rembrandt painted it in 1642: 363 by 437 cm of civic guardsmen stepping out of the dark, the largest painting in the collection. On the way to it, the Gallery of Honour lines up the rest of the Golden Age: Frans Hals, Jan Steen, Jacob van Ruisdael, and four Vermeers, including The Milkmaid, painted c. 1657-58. More than 2,000 Golden Age paintings sit among the 8,000 objects on display, drawn from a collection of one million. Since 2019 the Night Watch has been restored in public view as Operation Night Watch, behind glass in its own hall.
sections.caption: The Night Watch (1642) by Rembrandt van Rijn.
sections.heading: The Golden Age at the end of the gallery

sections.alt: Painted wall decoration in the Gallery of Honour
sections.body: The museum closed in December 2003 for a renovation that took almost ten years and cost 375 million euros. Seville architects Cruz y Ortiz worked under the motto 'Continue with Cuypers': the floors built into the courtyards in the 1960s came out, the glass roofs went over the atriums, and the painted decoration whitewashed in the 20th century was recovered. The reconstruction was completed on 16 July 2012, and the museum reopened on 13 April 2013, opened by Queen Beatrix. Cruz y Ortiz added the Asian pavilion in the garden, merging old and new in what the project architect called silent architecture.
sections.caption: Painted decoration in the Gallery of Honour.
sections.credit: Joseolgon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: Continue with Cuypers

sections.body:
The Rijksmuseum's most famous fictional moment is a heist that never happens. Advance publicity for Steven Soderbergh's Ocean's Twelve (2004) billed the Amsterdam job as a theft of the Night Watch from the Rijksmuseum. The finished film sends the crew after something else entirely: the world's oldest stock certificate, a 1602 Dutch East India Company share. The museum keeps its painting, and the mix-up says something true anyway: the Night Watch was the obvious prize to invent, because everyone already knows where it hangs.

The building itself is a fixture of Amsterdam's visual identity, its twin towers closing the Museumplein in countless films, series and photographs of the city. Cuypers's other great Amsterdam work, Centraal Station, shares its DNA, and the two buildings together define the 19th-century image of the capital. The museum drew 2,702,824 visitors in 2023. The museum that a king refused to open is now the building Amsterdam could not do without.
sections.heading: In the cultural conversation

timeline.text: Rembrandt paints The Night Watch, the painting the Gallery of Honour will one day be built around.
The government decides to found a national museum in The Hague.
The National Art Gallery opens in Huis ten Bosch, The Hague, with about 200 paintings and historic objects.
On the orders of King Louis Bonaparte, the museum moves to Amsterdam. Paintings owned by the city, including The Night Watch, join the collection.
The collection is housed in the Trippenhuis.
A design contest for a new building judges no entry good enough. Cuypers takes second place.
Cuypers wins the new contest; construction begins on 1 October 1876.
The museum opens on the Museumplein.
The fragment building is added southwest of the museum; it is later branded the Philips Wing.
The hall for The Night Watch is rebuilt.
Cruz y Ortiz renovation; the floors built into the courtyards in the 1960s are removed, and the Asian pavilion opens in 2013.
The renovated museum reopens, opened by Queen Beatrix.
Operation Night Watch begins: the painting is restored in public view.
